books.section: America Transformed into the Industrial Giant of the World (1870–1910)
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: Henry W. Grady, “The New South,” December 21, 1886

stimulus.text: “There was a South of slavery and secession—that South is dead. There is a South of union and freedom—that South, thank God, is living, breathing, growing every hour.” These words, delivered from the immortal lips of Benjamin H. Hill, at Tammany Hall, in 1866, true then and truer now, I shall make my text to-night. … The old South rested everything on slavery and agriculture, unconscious that these could neither give nor maintain healthy growth. The new South presents a perfect democracy, the oligarchs leading in the popular movement; a social system compact and closely knitted, less splendid on the surface, but stronger at the core; a hundred farms for every plantation, fifty homes for every palace; and a diversified industry that meets the complex needs of this complex age. … This is said in no spirit of time-serving or apology. The South has nothing for which to apologize. She believes that the late struggle between the States was war and not rebellion, revolution and not conspiracy, and that her convictions were as honest as yours.
stimulus.source_note: Henry W. Grady, “The New South,” address to the New England Society, New York, December 21, 1886. Public domain; wording and punctuation follow Life and Labors of Henry W. Grady (1890). The opening lines quote Georgia senator Benjamin H. Hill, speaking at Tammany Hall in 1866. Ellipses mark omissions between complete sentences.

stem: By “a hundred farms for every plantation, fifty homes for every palace,” Grady most likely means that the new South would have

options.text: more small farmers and homeowners, fewer great planters
a hundred times as much cotton as before
options.misconception: Grady is counting farms and homes, not bales of cotton.
Grady contrasts farms with plantations, not Southern with Northern owners.
Grady says homes, not palaces, and nothing about who built palaces.

rationales.A: Farms and homes stand against plantations and palaces: many small holders instead of a few great ones.
rationales.B: The numbers count farms and homes, not cotton.
rationales.C: Grady does not say who would own the plantations.
rationales.D: Grady promises homes for many, not palaces for anyone.
rationales.general:
Read the contrast, not just the numbers.
1. Grady sets farms against plantations and homes against palaces.
2. Plantations and palaces belong to a few rich owners.
3. A hundred farms and fifty homes mean many more ordinary owners.
4. Background from the books: Grady wanted a South of small farms and industry, not great plantations.
Remember: in a contrast, each side stands for a whole way of life.
